subject: mathematics
question_text: If A is the matrix with rows (cos θ, sin θ) and (−sin θ, cos θ), then show that for every positive integer n, Aⁿ is the matrix with rows (cos nθ, sin nθ) and (−sin nθ, cos nθ).

mark_split.label: Multiply Aᵏ by A and use the addition formulas
Conclude by the principle of induction

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.42, chapter 5 MATRICES, Short Answer question 10(ii). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+2+1 shape puts half the marks on the inductive multiplication because that is where the two compound-angle formulas are used and where every entry has to be recognised as cos or sin of (k+1)θ; the base case and the appeal to the principle of induction are short but each is a whole mark, since an answer missing either is not a proof. Independently checked before authoring: the claimed form was multiplied out at n = 1, 2 and 3, giving rows (cos θ, sin θ)/(−sin θ, cos θ), (cos 2θ, sin 2θ)/(−sin 2θ, cos 2θ) and (cos 3θ, sin 3θ)/(−sin 3θ, cos 3θ) — the formula exactly, with no leftover terms. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints eight short answers of which the student writes any six, each worth 4 marks, under the 2026-27 pattern; Matrices supplies one of them. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what you check first, what you assume, what two trigonometry formulas the multiplication needs, and how you finish.

steps.label: Check n = 1
steps.margin_note: First mark. Put n = 1 into the claimed form. Since 1θ is just θ, the claimed matrix becomes A itself, so P(1) is true.
steps.memory_tip: Base case first: n = 1 turns nθ into θ, so the claimed matrix is A itself.
lines: Let P(n) be the given statement about Aⁿ.
Putting n = 1 in the given form gives
cos 1θ = cos θ and sin 1θ = sin θ,
so it becomes A itself. P(1) is true.

recall.must_convey: That n = 1 is substituted into the claimed form, that one theta is just theta, and that the claimed matrix is then A itself.
accept: put n equals one and cos one theta is cos theta so the matrix is A itself
for n equals one the formula gives back the original matrix A
check the base case by substituting n equals one
n equals one pettina cos theta sin theta ne vasthundi, so A ne
the statement is true at n equals one because n theta becomes theta

steps.why: Induction needs a first true case to stand on. Here it is almost free, but leaving it out means the chain of implications starts from nothing.
common_mistakes: Skipping n = 1 because it looks obvious.
Writing the n = 1 matrix without saying it is the same as A.

steps.label: Assume for n = k
steps.margin_note: No mark of its own, but the next step multiplies this exact matrix by A, so write it out with kθ in every entry.
steps.memory_tip: Write the assumed matrix out with kθ in every entry — the next step multiplies that matrix by A.
lines: Assume P(k) is true for some k ≥ 1:

recall.must_convey: That the result is ASSUMED true for one integer n = k, with the assumed matrix written out in terms of k theta.
accept: assume it is true for n equals k with cos k theta and sin k theta in the entries
suppose A to the power k has the same shape with k theta
take the statement as true for some value k
n equals k ki result nijam ani anukuntam
let the formula hold for a general k
reject: assume it is true for all n
it is true for k plus one

steps.why: The assumption is about ONE value k. Assuming it for every n would assume the whole result, which is what the question asks you to prove.
common_mistakes: Saying "assume it is true for all n", which assumes what is being proved.
Writing nθ instead of kθ, so the next step has nothing new to prove.

steps.label: Multiply and use cos(A+B)
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Each of the four entries is a compound angle: cos kθ cos θ − sin kθ sin θ is cos(kθ + θ), and sin kθ cos θ + cos kθ sin θ is sin(kθ + θ). Then kθ + θ = (k+1)θ.
steps.memory_tip: Every entry is a compound angle: cos A cos B − sin A sin B is cos(A + B), and kθ + θ is (k+1)θ.

lines.text: A^{k+1} = A^{k} \cdot A = \begin{bmatrix} \cos k\theta & \sin k\theta \\ -\sin k\theta & \cos k\theta \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}

lines: Use cos A cos B − sin A sin B = cos(A + B)
and sin A cos B + cos A sin B = sin(A + B).
That is P(k+1). So P(k) ⇒ P(k+1).

recall.must_convey: That Aᵏ is multiplied by A, and that the four resulting entries are recognised as cos and sin of k theta plus theta by the compound-angle formulas, which is (k+1) theta.
accept: multiply A to the k by A and each entry becomes cos or sin of k theta plus theta
use cos A cos B minus sin A sin B equals cos A plus B on the entries
the products give cos k plus one theta and sin k plus one theta
compound angle formulas vaadithe k plus one theta vasthundi
row into column gives the addition formulas so the angle becomes k plus one theta
reject: find A to the k plus one
it is true for k plus one
heard_as: A to the k plus one

steps.why: The proof works only because the compound-angle formulas turn a product of two angles' ratios into a single angle kθ + θ. Without naming them the four entries are just unsimplified products.
common_mistakes: Writing cos kθ cos θ + sin kθ sin θ, which is cos(kθ − θ), not cos(kθ + θ).
Leaving the entries as products and never reaching (k+1)θ.
Losing the minus sign in the bottom-left entry.

steps.label: Conclude by induction
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Name the principle of mathematical induction. P(1) true plus P(k) leading to P(k+1) is exactly what the principle needs, and saying so is what makes this a proof rather than two calculations.
steps.memory_tip: Two facts earn the conclusion: P(1) is true, and P(k) leads to P(k+1). Name the principle.
lines: P(1) is true, and P(k) ⇒ P(k+1) for every k ≥ 1.
By the principle of mathematical induction, P(n)
is true for every positive integer n.

recall.must_convey: That both induction conditions hold and the principle of mathematical induction is named to give the result for every positive integer n.
accept: true for one and true for k plus one whenever true for k so by induction it holds for all positive integers
by the principle of mathematical induction the formula is true for every positive integer n
both conditions are satisfied so induction completes the proof
rendu conditions unnayi kabatti induction valla anni n ki nijam
the principle of induction gives the result for all n

steps.why: The earlier steps cover n = 1 and one implication only. The principle of induction is the theorem that turns those two facts into a statement about every positive integer, so it must be named.
common_mistakes: Writing only "hence proved" without naming the principle of induction.
Claiming the result for all real n; the proof covers positive integers only.
